Mathematics Education · Miami University

One course.
Fifteen weeks. Every feature.

A template for piloting the Math Ed portfolio inside a single methods course, using a Google Doc with tabs. Small enough to run this semester; shaped so it drops into the four-year Google Site later.

Template · Faculty piloting portfolios this semester; students in a single methods course

Selection. Reflection. Connection.

Definition 1.1 (ePortfolio). A curated collection of student-created work — for learning, assessment, and showcase — with reflection on each artifact and on the connections between them.

Corollary (Math Ed Portfolio). The same thing, organized around what a beginning mathematics teacher needs to be able to do. Without reflection it is a repository. With it, it is the argument, with evidence, that you are ready for your own classroom.

Principles for a pilotSlide 02

Same features, shorter loop

The working group's advice: start with the smallest manageable piece inside your locus of control. This is that piece.

Google Doc with tabs, not a site

One shared Doc per student: About & goals · Artifact 1 · Artifact 2 · Feedback log · Final reflection. No platform setup, instant instructor access.

Two artifacts, three reflections

Two full artifacts with reflections, plus a compare-and-contrast reflection between them. That is enough to show change inside one semester.

Feedback inside the Doc

Instructor comments live in the margin; students reply in the log tab within a week. The reply, not the comment, is graded.

Built to migrate

Tab headings match the Year 2 pages of the four-year Google Site. When the program adopts the full portfolio, students copy tabs into pages.

MILE alignmentSlide 03

The pilot is the course's MILE obligation, done well

MILE asks every Advanced Writing and ASC instructor to have students submit one artifact and a reflection to their portfolio shell. If the methods course carries an ASC designation, the pilot's Artifact 1 is that submission — and the Doc gives students more than the minimum.

The semesterSlide 04

Four phases, one Doc

Baseline in the first two weeks, an artifact cycle in each of the middle two phases, and a final reflection that reads the whole Doc back.

Weeks 1–2

Baseline

Copy the Doc · letter to end-of-semester self · philosophy v1 · three goals · muddiest point

Weeks 3–7

Artifact 1

Lesson plan with reflection · instructor feedback · reply · peer read

Weeks 8–12

Artifact 2

Student-work analysis or assessment · reflection · compare with Artifact 1 · feedback and reply

Weeks 13–15

Read it back

Reread the letter · grade the goals · philosophy v2 beside v1 · final integrative reflection

Every phase:one reflection tied to a specific artifact · one instructor comment answered in the log · goals revisited
Weeks 1–2Slide 05

Baseline

Everything later in the semester refers back to these two weeks. It takes one class session and one homework.

What you add

  • Copy the Doc template Five tabs, headings already in place. Share with the instructor as an editor. Confirm you have a MILE Google Site shell from UNV 101; create one if not.
  • Letter to your end-of-semester self Who are you as a math teacher right now? What do you want to be able to do by December? What worries you?
  • Teaching philosophy v1 Half a page. Kept exactly as written.
  • Three goals and a muddiest point Concrete enough to grade in Week 14.

What keeps learning going

  • Dated, never overwritten Each version is a new heading with the week number.
  • Instructor reads and asks one question Logged in the Feedback tab; the student's reply is the first graded entry.
  • Cue prior knowledge What experiences, identities, and strengths do you bring to teaching math? Where might they need repurposing?
  • Set the reply norm Instructor comments within a week; student replies within a week. Announced in the syllabus.
Reflection promptWhat do you already believe about how people learn mathematics — and where did that belief come from?
Weeks 3–12Slide 06

Two artifact cycles

Each cycle: make the artifact, reflect on it with a link to a specific part, get feedback, reply. The second cycle adds a comparison with the first.

What you add

  • Artifact 1 · lesson plan (MILE artifact) Standards alignment and anticipated student responses. Reflection: Process and Outcomes prompts. Copied to the Google Site shell as the course's MILE submission.
  • Artifact 2 · student-work analysis or assessment Anonymized responses sorted by strategy, or an assessment with results. Reflection: Outcomes and Integration prompts.
  • Compare-and-contrast reflection Artifact 2 beside Artifact 1: three differences and what they show about what you've learned.
  • Feedback log entries One instructor comment per artifact, each with a dated reply.

What keeps learning going

  • Like / not like How is analyzing student work like, and not like, planning the lesson? Like, and not like, being a student?
  • Peer read Trade Docs at Week 6; leave one comment the other must answer in their log.
  • Lesson wrapper If Artifact 1 is taught in a placement: how did you prepare, where did students struggle, what next?
  • Mid-semester goal check Week 8: reread the goals. One sentence each on progress.
Reflection promptPoint to one line in Artifact 2 that you could not have written before Artifact 1. What changed?
Weeks 13–15Slide 07

Read it back

The final reflection is written with the whole Doc open. It references specific tabs and quotes them.

What you add

  • Reread the Week 1 letter Grade each goal. Answer the muddiest point — or explain why it's still muddy.
  • Teaching philosophy v2 Rewritten, placed beside v1, with a note on what changed and what caused it.
  • Final integrative reflection Referencing both artifacts, the feedback log, and the letter: what can you do now that you couldn't in Week 1? What transfers to your next course or placement?
  • Letter to next-semester self Three goals for the next course. This becomes the first entry of the next cycle.

What keeps learning going

  • Integration prompt How does this semester's work connect to earlier courses and to your own schooling? How does it prepare you for student teaching?
  • Instructor's closing reply One paragraph on the growth the instructor sees, with tab references. The last entry in the log.
  • Exit permission The student keeps the Doc; the instructor is removed as editor, by the student, after grades post.
  • Migration note Artifact 1 and its reflection go to the MILE shell now. If the program adopts the four-year Site, copy every tab into the matching Year 2 page.
Reflection promptReread your Week 1 letter. Which of your worries turned out to be the right ones? What does the Doc show about how you handled them?

Running the pilotSlide 09

Materials to create, in order

From the Week 3 working-group homework: instructions, prompts, grading criteria. Three documents get the pilot running; two more make it repeatable.

1

The Doc template

Five tabs with headings and the reflection prompts already in place. Students copy it in Week 1.

2

Reflection prompts by week

Baseline, Artifact 1, Artifact 2, compare-and-contrast, final. Each names the artifact it must link to.

3

Grading criteria

Reflections graded on two things: is the claim tied to a specific place in the artifact, and did the student reply to feedback? Not on length.

4

Syllabus language

The reply-norm and the permission hand-off, in writing.

5

End-of-semester debrief

One page from the instructor: what worked, what to change, whether to propose the four-year version to the program. Bring it to MILO and the Howe Center faculty help sessions.

Sources: Miami ePortfolios Working Group, F'26, Weeks 2–3 (Google Doc with tabs; locus of control) · Lovett (2016) exam wrappers · Schraw (1998)
